utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. Unfortunately, Judge Thelin is unable to sit this morning, and we will continue as a Bench of two under the Rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Would you please stand and read aloud the affirmation on the card.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Good morning to all.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note, we can barely hear Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You're asked, Mr. Vasic, if you could keep your voice up.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm moving closer to the microphone. I think that's what's causing the problem. Thank you very much. I think this will be much better. Before I start asking away, can I please have the usher's assistance. If Ms. Usher could do something for me. I would like to submit a set of documents to each of the parties that we shall be using during the examination of this witness. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Would you please be so kind as to introduce yourself.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: My name is Zoran Basic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Sir, we both speak the same language. We are being interpreted for the benefit of the Chamber and all the parties. Therefore, could you please make a short pause after each of my questions before you start your answers, thereby enabling the interpreters to accurately interpret our exchanges. I'll do the same after each of your answers. The best thing perhaps would be for you to follow the cursor on the screen, on the monitor in front of you. As soon as a sentence is over, then you can start answering.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Sir, you are an officer of the JNA, a retired officer?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us about your military career, about your educational background and your specific jobs over the entire span of your career with the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: I have completed the highest possible military schools, including the All Peoples Defence school. I occupied all positions, platoon commanders up to chief, including stints with engineering units. I was always successful. Whenever there was a mission, I would complete it successfully. So my rates, my success rates, throughout my military career were as high as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. At the time you retired, which rank were you holding?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: At my retirement, I was a colonel, but I occupied the position equivalent to that of a general.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: To understand you correctly, when you say that the post you occupied would normally have required the rank of general, although you were a mere colonel at the time.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: No, not quite. I was the chief of my branch. However, based on my exceptional merit, I was in pay-group 6, which is equivalent to the pay of a general.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You mentioned that at one point in your career you served with the military district headquarters. Can you tell us which one and at which specific time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Having completed the All Peoples Defence college, I was appointed commander of a major unit in the 1st Military District. Three and a half years later I was appointed to a higher-ranking position with the military district. I was head of a branch. I could even say that I stayed there for too long. I occupied this position between 1969 and 1973, and I was again exceptionally successful in my work.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You say 1969 to 1973 you were the chief of branch or head of branch throughout that time. Which particular branch was that, and was it during the time period specified?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I have made an error. It was between 1976 and 1979. I was a brigade commander. Between 1979 and 1993, I was chief of branch in the Belgrade Military District, which is in terms of the area covered, the largest military district in the former Yugoslavia. It covered some of Serbia, some of Bosnia-Herzegovina and some of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You say the Belgrade Military District. You said the 1st Military District. I assume that this is what you had in mind. In the time relevant to this trial, 1990, 1991, based on what you've just told me, you were searching as chief in the branch of the 1st Military District. Which branch, can you tell us, sir.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Since 1979 and until 1993, I was the chief of engineers in the 1st Military District.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. As chief of engineers back in 1991, do you remember receiving any special assignments after the riots started in what used to be the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Yes. At the time, those of us who were more experienced officers were sent on certain missions. Just to give you one example, in 1991 there was a visit to Mrkovci and Vinkovci. I did go into Vinkovci, actually. And we were monitoring the situation. It was a complex assignment, a complex mission, but I was in charge of teams that went to the Vukovar front and the Vinkovac front, that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You say you were present in this area, and your mission was to monitor the situation. Who were you assisted by on this mission, and who were you cooperating with? Who were you working with at this time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure if you mean the situation when the breakaway, the secession began. Is that what you're referring to, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: By all means. I'll need to clarify this. You told us about monitoring the situation. This monitoring, was that before armed clashes broke out or after?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: I think it was before armed clashes broke out. Since this part of Croatia was under our jurisdiction, our units were deployed in Osijek, in Donje Mikojac, Vukovar, and so on and so forth. I as chief received certain assignments as an operative body to visit those garrisons and to assist wherever necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, if you remember, did you continue to assist and advise these garrisons once armed clashes had broken out and the fight for secession had begun as you put it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: You're quite right. We had our own units under our jurisdiction over which we exercised command, but we also had jurisdiction over some other units within the military district. It was for this reason that certain activities were pursued pursuant to orders from the military district itself, and we worked with those units.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This role you played at the time, did that cover Croatia in it's entirety or, rather, that area of Croatia which was under the jurisdiction of the 1st Military District?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Or, rather, how long did you stay in this position? I mean in relation to units subordinate to the command of the 1st Military District. Is this something you remember, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Of course I do. How wouldn't I? Back in 1992, more specifically in August, I retired. Up until that point in time, until the very last day, in fact, I was in charge over the operative units of the 1st Army as well as the TO units coordinating with the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At this time, as a representative of the command of the 1st Military District, did you relate in the same way to the units of the guards motorised division that were deployed near Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you, perhaps you're misexpressing yourself. The 1st guards division if that's the one you had in mind, or, rather, the brigade of the Federal Secretariat, do you mean the one or the other?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I'm waiting for the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I mean the guards division that was involved in the fighting in Vukovar in September, 1991.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Yes. You're quite right. I had two many commitments, in fact, towards that unit in terms of preparing the unit as well as carrying out the actual assignments of the 1st Guards Division. I have to point out at that I made several visits there in order to sort out a variety of situations in Mrkovci, Pavlovci, Bogdanovci. Furthermore, I was myself in Mrkovci where the TO units were holding the area. I was there myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you report to the command of the 1st Military District about these activities and, if so, how?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you -- I apologise. Let me tell you. To be the chief of branch is a great commitment, and the link to the Chief of Staff and the commander is direct, which means that one needs to report every single move and every single action that one takes in writing. We had our own codes. We regularly submitted these reports. It would be less than serious for a person in that position not to keep reporting. The entire command would be briefed about everything that had occurred, regularly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: This system of reporting that you have mentioned, was this established practice with the command of the 1st Military District, and was the same thing done by other bodies with other commitments and duties, other chiefs of branches?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. I have to tell you this: In the evening decisions were made for the following day. Mr. Mrksic and all the others know that, because they were under our authority, and they pursued our orders, and every evening we would be debriefed, and then we would correct our previous orders and issue new orders. All the organs did absolutely the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, sometime in mid-November, did you receive a very specific task relative to the completion of combat activities in the Borovo-Vukovar sector in addition to the tasks that you had or any tasks that were relative to Eastern Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: I monitored that task constantly, and that was the focus of our monitoring. And I participated all the time in those efforts on the Vinkovci-Osik access. So this was nothing new. When this activity ended, we continued our supervision of those units, and we continued having commitments towards those units. I received an order from the Secretariat for National Defence to take urgent measures for de-mining, return of population to the territory, cleaning of the terrain, and this was a very complex task, and it was a burning issue, one of the most difficult tasks in my career.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. Can we please be shown Exhibit number 1D6 from the 65 ter list, ERN is 0D0003. I apologise. 1D16 is the document number, and the ERN now is 0D000350. The English version is 0D000351. The B/C/S version is 0D000348, and the last two digits of the next document are 49. Thank you. Sir, do you have the document before you on the screen? Do you also have a hard copy?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Since we all have the hard copy version in B/C/S, maybe we could have the English version on the screen. Sir, I'm referring you to your hard copy version. I'm sure it will be easier for you to follow that rather than the copy on the screen. Can you please tell us whose order is this? Who issued this order? The number in the heading is 1614-176.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: This order was issued by the command of the military district, and this was something that preceded the order of the Federal Secretariat. The order was necessary because the deployment was necessary because certain orders had to be taken to clean up the area, to de-mine the area and everything else that accompanied the situation. So the unit started doing at that as soon as they received this order, and three days later a new order arrived and this would be relevant to supplement the previous order and to enlarge the scope of activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. What preceded the issuance of this order on clean-up? What problems preceded this order? What prompted the command of the 1st Military District to set up a commission that would be engaged in the issues of the clean-up of the terrain that this issue -- that this order is relevant to?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you this: All our rules, instructions that dealt with the issue of clean-up were so minor that they only dealt with sporadic problems. There were no wide-reaching rules. At the end of my task I proposed that instructions should be drafted for the critical stages where works had been undertaken in a larger territory that had been struck by war or some ecological disasters. This did not exist. Everything that happened with these units -- I must tell you that the biggest problem -- problems stemmed from the -- from the fact that dead bodies had not been cleaned up, that carcasses had not been cleaned up, and this was all why we had to do something urgently, and this is why this order was issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you please speak a little slowly, because our interpreters are having a rather difficult time if we speed up. Can you -- you've mentioned some obstacles or barricades that had been put up by somebody. Who was it who put up those barricades that prompted the command of the 1st district to issue this order and to undertake orders?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: In this war, obstacles were placed in very different ways. No record was kept of these obstacles, and no attention was paid to the Geneva Conventions. We thought that members of the Croatian National Guard were not very well-versed in placing obstacles, but they did it in a very devious way. They destroyed bridges in the Mrkovci sector, in the Nijemci sector, and all the while up to the placing gas tanks, activating gas tanks. They would place mines in a four-storey building, and that was terrible. I was astonished when I saw around Dudik, the memorial park in Dudik that they placed mines in a very expert way, that those were very, very sophisticated mines that inflicted a lot of damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this answer. Can you please slow down a little when you're speaking for the benefit of the interpreters. You were saying when giving your answer that there were certain events that took place and that went beyond some rules that were in place at that time. Who the perpetrators of those offences were? Who placed those obstacles beyond the scope of any rules?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Of course the perpetrator is well known. My authority was well pronounced when it came to the system of placing obstacles. This was done in such an expert and sophisticated way. For example, the blowing up of the bridge in Nijemci. This was a very sophisticated act. Minefields were placed in the same way. But I have to tell you one more thing. There were very professional officers in the Croatian National Guard who all completed their education in Karlovac and engineers school. The chief of engineers in the national guard of Croatia was Tolice who was in charge of placing obstacles around the entire area of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I'm still waiting for the interpretation to end. Tell me, who was it who was in charge of the territory where these obstacles were placed during the armed conflict. Do you have that information? Which side was in charge of that territory? In whose hands was it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Of course I know, because I was deployed in that territory before the armed conflict and -- during the armed conflict up to the fall of the Jovanovci-Bijelo Brdo line going all the way up to Tenjavera [phoen]. It was the Croatian National Guard forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's go back to the order that you have before you. In paragraph two of this order, the objective of setting up of this commission is indicated. Can you please read this part very slowly. I'm referring to the paragraph in the order number 1614-176 on the setting up of this commission. Do you have that in front of you in hard copy?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: The second paragraph speaks about the need to set up the commission, and can you please read for us why the commission was set up?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: You see, we had to comply with the order of the Federal Secretariat. Our task, according to that order, was like the command of the 1st District received information from the ground on the situation. That was very difficult at the time. This reflected on the Federal Secretariat that issued this order and said in the order urgently secure the area, find the dead and the wounded, remove mines and explosives, de-mine the fields, remove the explosives and mines on the ground. And this was all necessary so as to enable people to go back to their homes as soon as possible. Conditions had to be created for that. I can tell you from experience, because this was in a certain way my wish, to see how many citizens of Vukovar and Borovo would return. And I must tell you that by the beginning of December, over 15.000 people returned to Vukovar. At the time, we did not count heads of Serbs, Croats, Ruthenians. We were Yugoslav officers and people were equal to us. We created a security and safety. I can tell you what the press wrote about our successes in the territory at the time, but I can only tell you that we have contributed to the well-being of these people to a very large extent. And I believe that this order was a very valuable one and that it achieved its goal.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. A commission was set up pursuant to this order, and in the order it says that a commission is set up in the following composition: Colonel Zoran Basic, Colonel Bratislav Stasic, Colonel Savo Djelasan, and Colonel Svetislav Kostic. Can you please tell us if this was indeed the make-up of the commission and who the president of the commission was?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: This was the composition of the commission, save for the last member, who for, I don't know what reason, did not attend the work of the commission but the first through were there. They were all experts in the area of security, engineering. In other words, we were very professional, and we were well-equipped to perform that task. And I was appointed president of that commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I would like to draw your attention as well as the attention of my learned friends to the last paragraph of this order by the command of the 1st District setting up the commission, and this is immediately above the signature of Vladimir Stojanovic, the Chief of Staff, and it says here that on the basis of the proposals and suggestions as well as the collected data an organisational order should be drafted for the implementation of this task. I would like to know who should have been in charge of drafting this organisational order for the implementation of this task. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: You saw my initials in the corner, ZB. That's one thing. And I was the one who was best equipped to do that job, because I had spent most time in the territory, and having been familiar with the situation, I could have drafted such an order that would find its use in all units. I was the one who could represent the reality of the situation in the best possible way.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: As far as I understand, and please correct me if I'm wrong, you drafted this organisational order for implementing this task adopted by the command of the 1st Military District on the 23rd of November, 1991. Is that true, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I move this order of the 1st Military District command, 1614-176, ID16, be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number 758, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: After the commission was established, sir, where did you go, you and I expect members of your commission? Where did you go, and where were you billeted?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Since I was monitoring the situation, whenever a need began to bud, it wasn't difficult to get me there in order to organise everything. Although an order was being drafted by the Federal Secretariat, orders were still being issued, brief ones, succinct ones, so everything could be prepared. The important thing was to get there as soon as possible. Winter was encroaching gradually, and the difficulty faced by those on the ground was considerable. Therefore, we had to roll up our socks and get down to actually working on the ground. We were told to go to Dalj and stay with the 12 Corps, the late Bratic. That's where we were. On the 22nd and 23rd, we had completed organising all of our forces, all of our units. These units, these forces were exceptionally qualified, and this was important in view of the complex tasks that we were facing. Our powers were exceptionally extensive. No one would have been allowed to limit our movement or our remit. It was down to us to show initiative in terms of organising work and life in the area and to be expeditious too.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I was just about to ask, was it your work, your task, of all things, that assumed a formal aspect because of the order that was issued on the 23rd of November, 1991. And now, if we could please have a 65 ter document, Defence document, on our screens. 1D10. The ERN of the English being 0D000469. My apologies. It's my mistake. The ERN 0D000373 through 0375. The B/C/S is 0D000371 through 72. Thank you. I hope we all have a hard copy of this order. Sir, so should you. You should have a hard copy in front of you. This is strictly confidential. Number 1614-182. The 1st Military District command, the 23rd of November, 1991. Would you be so kind, sir, as to have a look at this order and tell us what it says. Based on which other orders was this order produced, and does it not amount to the same thing as the organisational order for the implementation of your task that you talked about a while ago?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. This is certainly a basis for an order to be drafted. You know something? It's pretty clear cut in the army who gives directives and who hands them out and it is in line that that you have to draft orders. The timing is important, and you have to know what forces are available. You will probably be asking another question later about the forces that were grouping there. That was the most complex aspect, to gather them and to get them organised.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much indeed, sir. In your response you mentioned this Federal Secretariat for All People's Defence. I would like to draw your attention to the very beginning of the order on the consideration now, 1614-182, and the portion entitled "Signals." And then there is this order by the Federal Secretariat, strictly confidential, 693-106. What I want to know is is this the order that you refer to later -- earlier in one of your answers as the fundamental order for clearing the terrain which was eventually followed by the 1st Military District command?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Indeed. With certain provisos, obviously. There is an outline of what else needs doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We're getting to the question you raised yourself a while ago. What were the forces that were under the command of the commission headed by you? What were the forces involved in the implementation of this task, and what was the area in which this activity took place?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: The military district command, the SSNO, in order to have these tasks implemented needed to provide appropriate assistance. There was a great variety of forces. This was a very complex situation. So one thing I'd like to point out is the JNA provided the investigating magistrates from the Belgrade military court led by Saljic Milo investigative magistrate and his assistants. Further, a body from the 50th medical regiment held by Ljubomir Sljivovic, and then bodies from the Military Medical Academy, pathology institute, headed by Major Zoran Stankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may continue but there is one name that has been misrecorded and just to keep from losing the thread, please, when you pronounce names and unit, just try to go a little more slowly so we can get it all in. The 5th medical regiment --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: No, no, no, no. The associated preventive medical detachment from Svezdara headed by Ljubomir Videnovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will have to really sink our teeth into this. We have to pronounce the names of these units slowly because we have a great deal of confusion in the transcript. I will do it all over again. You were speaking about this medical unit. Please tell us slowly which medical unit and tell us slowly who it was held by? But slowly so everybody understands what you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Organs of the 50th protection preventive medical detachment led by Lieutenant Colonel Ljubo Videnovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you for trying. As you continue enumerating these various units, please do it in perhaps the same way as now, slowly.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Organs of the Military Medical Academy. The pathology institute led by the then Major Zoran Stankovic. Further, units for immediate implementation of assignments, the 305th Engineering Brigade. Further, the 24th Engineers Regiment. Further, the 813th Engineers Regiment, its numerical strength being about 3.150 officers and soldiers. And about 138 pieces of engineering equipment. Further, a company for biological, chemical, and -- protection and atomic warfare from the 246th regiment of the atomic, biological and chemical defence, as well as a platoon from Belgrade city's defence system, which was another JNA unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We need to stop here before we go on with this unit that was outside the JNA. The ones that you mentioned as being inside the JNA, part of the JNA, this particular unit, was it placed at your disposal and sent to your area, especially after the organisational order was received when you realised how many different things you would have needed and what exactly, were they placed at your disposal by the 1st Military District command?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Yes, all these units were placed under my direct command. It was a fortunate circumstance that these were units that had been organised on the ground even before this time. They were just taken away from their normal units, larger units of which they were part and placed under my command.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Were these units, too, in the area covered by the 12th corps, which is where your headquarters was before you set out for this operation?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Would you please be so kind and tell us what the units were that were not formally part of the JNA, these other units that were involved in carrying out the task of which you were in charge?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: As for the external units, non-JNA units, we had the following units: Interior Ministry of the Republic of Serbia; SUP of Vojvodina, the province of Vojvodina. Further, investigating magistrate from Novi Sad. Further, doctors from the pathology institute of the Novi Sad hospital. Whenever necessary, the -- we could have had more, which sometimes we required. There was a task, an initiative, at one point in time to enlist the assistance of the Red Cross from that area as well as other forces. There was little we could do about that, but we had some Red Cross people from Borovo Naselje who helped us clear the ground. But there was little we could do in order to get that. But we had our own manpower. We had our own qualified people, our own technicians and everything else that was required, in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You say you enlisted the assistance of the Red Cross from Borovo Selo, but did you also enlist the help of the Vukovar TO staff?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: We worked with the assistant commander for logistics, Antic, from the TO staff. He backed us and he helped us, but it was more us who were helping them on certain assignments, but rather than them assisting us. We couldn't even get ordinary citizens to help us clear the bodies and bury the bodies. Eventually we had to gather a number of volunteers and pay them daily rates to help us with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: When you talk about this assistance, cooperation, I don't know what I should call it, with the assistant commander of the TO staff of logistics, do you know where this headquarters was, or this logistics base of the Vukovar TO, its location?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Of course I know. I was in touch with them all the time. Antic was stationed at Velepromet. This entire territorial structure that was unified was there. The Municipal Assembly was a street away from there. I think Vukum [phoen] Radic was the chairman of the Municipal Assembly, and I knew all of them as the Assembly was being set up. I knew all of these people because I needed all the help I could get. They helped to the best of their abilities, but we could hardly have expected more.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: When I look at this order that we have in front of us, if I look at item 1, which describes the composition of the units placed under your command for this mission, it says: "Organs of the SAO Krajina of Slavonija, Baranja and Zapadonja Srem [phoen]." Can you tell us which organs of the autonomous province are these, the ones referred to here?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: We had nothing to do with them and no help from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So although they're specifically stated in this order by the 1st Military District command, you still got no support from these autonomous province bodies. Can you tell us at least which organs or which bodies the reference is to?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: I believe that the reference here is more to organs of the vicinity of Vukovar, Slavonija where we had Borovo Naselje, where we had Borovo Selo, major settlements. And it was from Borovo Selo of all places that we received the most assistance from ordinary citizens, from the locals, because they were the ones maintaining the siege and taking into account everything that needed doing, but we didn't get any help from anyone else, not even an undertaker who could have helped us bury the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Basic, I would like to go back to what you mentioned before as someone being within your group, the investigators of the military court who had their own jobs and the investigators of the civilian judiciary. What were their jobs and what were their assignments really?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Had we not had them with us, we could not have legally worked on any of the jobs, especially when it came to the discovering of graves, mass graves, identification of bodies. This was all their job. We set up such groups in order to provide them with protection, freedom of work, and physical protection when they performed their duties. In order for them to perform their jobs, we had to help them, and there was a harmony between us. We never had a single problem whether it was the fact that we all loved our work, that we wanted to carry the job through, that we took pride in what we did, I don't know what was the cause of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Sir, was the task of these investigative bodies in addition to what you have mentioned and that was the legal way to exhume bodies, was their task also to process perpetrators of crimes if such perpetrators were discovered?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was the case, of course. And they helped us with that. We had very few situations of them working beyond that scope. There was so much work here that they couldn't do much else. And this part of the job we gave to Antic, who was the commander of the logistics in Vukovar and they also processed thefts and other crimes. I don't know to what extent and how this continued.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Tell me, these bodies, including the ones that we are talking about right now, were they also responsible to the command of the 1st District for the implementation of their tasks?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Let me put it this way: We knew exactly how far our authorities went. That's why we had Alan Piovic [phoen], the little Saljic, and so on and so forth. They were our right hand in that respect. All of the authorities that touched upon those issues we handed over to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: The persons that you just mentioned, were they actually investigative judges who were on the ground and who were in charge of anything that had to do with law?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Tell me please, your commission that was in involved in the task of clearing and clean-up, what part of the area were you responsible for and in which period of time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: When the command issues an order, they don't know what the scope of the job will be. The winter was very harsh. It was icy. It was very difficult to dig up the victims' bodies and identify them. Those were all consequences of the winter. And up to 20th of February, we managed to perform the total scope of the de-mining jobs. We did the entire clear-up. A lot of people returned to their homes. This -- the Vukovar Hospital was completed and restored to its function. What we did not accomplish by February we put forward to March. Let me just give you an example. About 1.350 victims were identified and 300 remained for identification. We collected all the bodies at Ciglana where they were kept and we were in constant conflict with our pathologist and we dealt with all these problems. This whole mission was completed by the end of April, 1992, for all the various reasons that I've just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let's go -- we shall go back to our -- to your particular task a bit later. Can you please look at the order that we are talking about. That is strictly confidential order number 1614-182 paragraph 8 of this order which speaks about the military investigative organs of the 1st District. Let me read and then you will explain the meaning of this paragraph. It says in this paragraph as follows: "The military investigative organ of the 1st District will determine a necessary number of persons for all the tasks relative to the identification of bodies and other tasks from -- stemming from their authorities." Is this what you were talking about, and that is that the investigative judge was in charge of the tasks of identification and everything else that accompanied exhumation and other things all the way up to the prosecution of the perpetrator if there is a reasonable doubt that there was a crime involved in the death of the -- that body?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: You are right. We were assisted by the organs of the Supreme Court. At certain points they came to provide advice and this was the mutual assistance that we provided to each other. And I believe that the military investigative bodies did a very good job. I don't know whether their competence -- whether it was in their purview to prosecute perpetrators or not. However, they had a very serious task, and it was very difficult for them to go beyond that task and prosecute thieves or perpetrators of minor crimes, but we knew that, and they did their job very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Basic. I would now like to draw your attention to paragraph 12 of this order in which it says that communications chief of the 1st District will plan communications of the Operative Group south for the purposes of the city command and the commission. Does that mean that what had been used before by the Operative Group south is now being transferred to the command of the city of Vukovar and the commission for clear-up?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: This was indispensable, because the garrison command, the commander of the 80th Motorised Brigade, Vojnovic, he assumed duties of the garrison commander. Second of all, our commission was in the entire territory of Slavonija, not only in Vukovar but everywhere where anything appeared. I am referring to the general area of Vukovar. That's why we had to have communications means. We had to be in contact with the 1st Guards Brigade and so on and so forth. The system had to function, and it had to be enlarged to other structures that had been established in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Page 23, line 15, the name recorded is "Vujovic". It should be "Vojnovic". You've just mentioned the territory in which your commission was active, which brings me to paragraph 17 of that same order, the last paragraph in the order in which it says that the mission commander will submit daily reports to the commission on the implementation of all tasks in various microlocations, and the commission, in its turn, will regularly report to the command about the situation on the ground. Can you please explain how you as the head of this commission report -- reported to the district command? In what form were your reports, and how often were they submitted?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Our commission was billeted in Ciglane near Velepromet across the road from Vupik. This was our command post. In the morning we organised the beginning of work. We organised ourselves. Around 1600 hours, just before dusk, we had to stop working to pull people back because there was fire all over the town. This task of collection, as soon as it was processed at the level of the commission, it was coded through the garrison command, and it was sent to the command of the military district. And this was what happened every day. In drastic cases I would report urgently by means of radio telephone to the commander, because I was in constant contact with him. Secondly, at the level of the garrison command we organised a meeting, a regular meeting involving the president of the command of the 1st Guards Brigade, Mr. Sljivic. He was there at every meeting. We met regularly in order to assist each other in all the relevant issues. The commander was not very experienced, and that's why he benefited from our assistance. Then once a week I would meet with the military commander and his assistants to discuss all the issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you please repeat who was there in addition to the commander of the military district, which assistants were there? But slowly.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: The commander of the military district could not have done anything without his assistants and those were assistant commanders for logistics, the chief of medical department, the chief of technical department, the chief of security. Mile Babic was in that post at the time. These are the bodies who were of immediate assistance to the commander for all the relevant -- relevant issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would tender this document bearing number ID 1D10 for admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: With the Exhibit number 759, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You were talking about reporting to the commander and his assistants. Did you report to any other bodies in the 1st Military District about any problems or irregularities that you encountered on the ground? In other words, problems that happened that you were informed about, problems that would be relative to volunteers, members of the ZNG?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: We were very good colleagues and we cooperated very well, and the commander of the military district issued an order that every form of assistance should be extended to me. And this did not have to be reiterated. As soon as I requested something from the assistant, any assistant, this would be implemented immediately. There were no confrontations there. There was no position on anybody's part to any of the requests that I may have had.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I would now like to ask you whether you knew an officer, Colonel Petkovic. Can you tell us who he was at the relevant time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Colonel Petkovic was a chief of security of the military district. He was in Sid. Actually, he was not chief. Milan Babic was chief, but he was his assistant in Sid. In critical situations, I had to call him in order to deal with some issues, to resolve certain problems. Sometimes problems were major so he had to come over. They thought that we could deal with everything, and we could. We dealt with issues that were within our purview, but we had him who could turn up and provide us with assistance if needed. He would come from -- all the way from Sid to help us.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that when you informed him about certain problems he was not very willing to help you solve them, although he was informed about problems that existed on the ground?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: You spotted that very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, please, Mr. Basic, the commission that you led, did it meet every day to consider plans for more efficient and better implementation of your mission? And when it came to the implementation of your mission, did you ask for support from companies across Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Let me put it this way: Our commission worked in a very responsible way. We did not need any help from elsewhere in Yugoslavia, because the command of the military district was a very strong organisation, and if they could not solve the problem, nobody could. Several times we addressed SAO Krajina, but we did not receive any help. The Minister of Health was there who did not help us in any way. He did not help us in an adequate way, although these were his people. The president, who had come from Bosnia, actually from Krajina, he was in Erdut. He also did not help us in any way. Sometimes as he was passing by he would stop in his vehicle just to ask us how we were doing, but he did not help us. We did not need his help, as a matter of fact. We were glad when he stopped. But we could deal with all the problems ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: We'll return to the specific assignments of your commission later on to discuss them in greater detail. Now I want to know about repairing buildings that were of public interest in order to get as many people as possible back. Where did you find the construction materials necessary for these repairs, and who was helping you with that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: You know, to be a chairman of a commission you need a lot of understanding, a lot of knowledge. You need to be aware of what is possible. For example, just for the Vukovar Hospital, I picked up a power generator that weighed 600 kilos myself from a pit in the ground for it to be used there, and then I took several trucks -- truckloads of glass from the Novi Sad glassworks for the Vukovar Hospital. I got 80 of the best people, stone masons, concrete workers, stone cutters, from all the brigades, and then we set up a working group to help mend the hospital. A month later the hospital was up and running and in a position to perform even the most complex times of surgery. The chairman of the commission and all members were not there to stand by and idly watch. They had to blanch headlong into the tasks facing them. I knew every single building from roof to basement. I knew every single construction site. I knew every single street. The length of all these roads, the total length, was 218 kilometres. We cleared all of these. Not a single mine left. Roads fit for travel. All the vehicles that had been destroyed, but now it was all clear, and most of the debris was near the bus terminal, and we later took this to Odzak. But we certainly did a great deal to help the returnees, to the people returning to Vukovar. Just as all the principal streets. We did the mending ourselves. We mentioned all these houses for the citizens, all the principal buildings, but they helped too.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Before we head for our break, just one thing. What about the water pipes in Vukovar, the water supply system? Was this badly damaged, and how long did you take to get it up and running again?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: The water supply system was entirely destroyed. Just to give you an example, we built artesian wells for the Vukovar Hospital, but meanwhile we also helped clean the water supply system. We introduced high voltage electricity with a company from Vojvodina. We had people doing this, distributing the cables, putting up pylons. Until the final confrontation there was high voltage. So Vukovar was up and running again. It got a new lease of life. It had running water, electricity, everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Basic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe this would be a convenient time for our first break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasic. We will resume at just after a quarter to eleven.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I know there have been problems with the interpreters. I hope that now the sound is better. If so, I would like to continue. Sir, before the break we spoke about the assignments of your commission in Vukovar, Borovo, and parts of Eastern Slavonia. You enumerated for us the units involved, the units that were under your command while you were carrying out all those tasks. At one point in time, I think you said, and it may have been a mistake, you mentioned the 1st Guards Brigade. I suppose you meant the 1st guards division, since as far as I know there was no such thing as the 1st Guards Brigade.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: I think it was an error in terms of the authority of the military district over the brigade, and the 1st guards division is the 1st guards division.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, you spoke about the fact that you succeeded in record time to get the hospital up and running. I would now like to show you the photograph that has an exhibit number. The photograph shows the hospital. Can we please have Exhibit 170. This is photograph number 11. The ERN number is 00531266. Mr. Basic, can you tell what's in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the side entrance to the hospital building near the basement. I spent some time there. I was there several times surveying the situation, and I have to say in my opinion the hospital had been prepared in some way for combat operations and used for combat operations. I went to all the rooms, and I surveyed the entire situation. In addition to this, the basement and the first floor had water mattresses on which they slept with hundreds of litres of water, and this water was used for combat. That's my opinion. I have to tell it like it is. My friend and colleague was the director of the hospital, Ivezic. I have to say that hospital did not put up a single soldier, did not hospitalise a single soldier, but in a month's time we had the hospital full of soldiers, wounded persons, people who had lost their limbs. One thing is for certain. I'm familiar with the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can we clarify something, please? You said that as of the 23rd you started clearing up. I suppose it's after that date that you got to the hospital, the hospital building. Can you confirm that for me, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Another matter which I would like to have clarified. You gave us your opinion on what the hospital had been used for. Would you agree with me that you saw no weapons in the hospital when you came? This was several days after Vukovar had been taken.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Indeed. We pulled out a number of bodies from the hospital, dead bodies, but one thing that was particularly exceptional was there were two common graves across the way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I object to the questions in relation to the hospital. My learned friend knows that we have indicated that the summaries that we received were inadequate. We received a proofing note at 3.50 this morning, which is extensive, and there is no reference, as far as I can see, to anything about the hospital. We submit if this topic is going to be dealt with, it should have been in the summary so that we have the proper and appropriate notice of any of these areas or this specific area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it wasn't my intention to speak about the hospital, and I wouldn't have unless the witness had confirmed about them getting the hospital up and running in a month's time. And I will not inquire into any further circumstances regarding the hospital, especially in view of the fact that the witness only arrived at the hospital several days after the fall of Vukovar, which makes it entirely irrelevant for our purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm glad you used those words, because that is the fact. A number of the matters being dealt with by the witness have no relevance to the issues we're trying. They may be very important to the witness, having regard to his role, but they're not going to assist us in the trial of this matter. The evidence concerning the hospital will not be taken into account by the Trial Chamber in its deliberations.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can we now please move on to what I indicated would be another subject matter for us to tackle, that is the mines lying about Vukovar and the areas that were mined. Can you specify the areas that you worked in when you were clearing these mines, and can you tell us what sort of explosives were found? Can you tell us about whether there was any system to these mines being laid and distributed, in the briefest possible terms, please.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: If we look at the general area of Vukovar and Borovo, the entire area was strewn with mines and explosives. The clearing was done in a systematic way in order to get the area back to normal as soon as possible. Now, as to the system that was used while laying these mines, we cleared 16.000 anti-tank mines in Vukovar, the airport, and Borovo Naselje. Seven tonnes of explosives, gas cylinders, that sort of thing. It was dreadful. It was dreadful the sort of explosives that were concealed all around the area, especially near the major roads such as the Borovo-Dalj-Bogojeva [phoen] road. There were lots of mines there. The Vukovar-Sotin-Sid road, the Vukovar-Bogdanovci road, the Vukovar-Negoslavci road. Likewise these were the directions in which our brigade was moving. The Vukovar-Brsadin road, the Vukovar-Trpinje road. In Vukovar itself there were lots of obstacles near the bridges, the Vuka River, near the Marina. That area was affected to a large degree. Also, another area where this problem was particularly pronounced was the area around Luzac, also Mitnica. These were areas where the most obstacles were found.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What I want to know is downtown Vukovar. I'm particularly interested in that. Could we have Exhibit 256 brought up, photograph number 6. Exhibit 256, photograph number 6. The ERN is 00531236. Thank you. We have it on our screens. Mr. Basic, what does this photograph show?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: This is the bus terminal, the market, and then the road to the hospital on the left and then the road to the department store. Also heading for the hospital there is the marina, and this area had lots of mines and other sorts of obstacles in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If you can please continue to speak slowly. I think the second part of your testimony in the morning was much, much better in those terms. And if the usher could hand the witness what my learned friend usually calls the magic pen so he can mark for us the areas of downtown Vukovar that were mined and booby-trapped before the team that arrived cleared the mines.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: The bridge over the river Vuka. There are two bridges. The marina, this area, and I just have to tell you, this street, the road to the hospital, it was all booby-trapped as well. So this is the area shown in the photograph. Mitnica, Oljinica [phoen], all these areas were booby-trapped all over. Oljinica is to the left of the hospital on the way to Luzac. That area was quite booby-trapped as well. We lost two soldiers there from the 305th brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could you please put a number 1 in the area where the bridges were, per se number 2 where the marina was that you mentioned. Number 3, you said. Okay. Number 2 --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Where the bus terminal was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What about this arrow in the direction of the hospital? Can you put a number 4 there, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I move that this be admitted into evidence, the map as marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, it will be received with Exhibit number 760.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Basic -- we won't be needing Ms. Usher's help with the photograph for the time being. A little later perhaps. Thank you. Mr. Basic, can you tell us how long your team took to clear the Vukovar area and its surroundings, to clear the mines, and when was this mission completed, roughly speaking?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Vukovar was divided into areas as well as Borovo Naselje, as far as the Bulgarian cemetery and Vucedol. Vucedol and the surrounding vineyards were booby-trapped to a large extent, and each unit was given an area. The 305th brigade was given Borovo Naselje because that was the strongest unit, and they were capable of carrying out this mission. They were well trained with some experienced senior officers, and their numerical strength was the greatest of all the units there. The 24th got the area to the right, Oljinica. And the 813th was assigned the area near the Bulgarian cemetery, Dubrava, Jakvolac [phoen], Ovcara, and that general area. So that the entire room was enveloped. They got themselves organised and they finished sometime in December, on the 25th or the 28th. Some of the units were leaving the area by this time and were on their way back.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, when was it safe for people, for civilians, to move about the centre of Vukovar without fearing that they would come across a mine?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Listen, we used Free Slavonija, the radio station, on a daily basis. Every three or four days I would publicly announce the rules of conduct for the citizens. We were telling them that the situation was quite complex and that there were many dangers of being injured and wounded. So we took all kinds of measures to ensure safety. We instructed citizens to inform us as soon as possible if they noticed anything in their houses, in their gardens. We had small intervention platoons that would be available to intervene immediately should there be any explosive found. I think that we had very brave people there who were very loyal to us and reported things to us. We even conducted some exhumations upon receiving information and found some people. It is quite certain that the commanders guaranteed that their sectors were all complete, and we had no fatalities in those areas. Yes, there were some mines planted and there were cases where neighbours did that to each other and peoples limbs were blown off, but that's another matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What you said about the commanders, did you have in mind December?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. December. Late November and December.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In addition to the work on de-mining and the work on ensuring safe passage through the region, your commission and units subordinated to it also were duty-bound to remove carcasses so that there would be no infection spreading around.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us in which locations carcasses were buried?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Not only in the Vukovar region but throughout the entire Slavonian and down towards Nijemci we came across a terrible situation in relation to dead animals. Why? Because there was a lot of food for them but no water, and in Vukovar there was a great amount of dead animals. Some cattle died in Jakupovac and Ovcara in great numbers, so we buried those carcasses immediately. And then there was some cattle that died in Vukovar itself. We had a prevention platoon, and they had a large number of vehicles, loaders, and they would transport those carcasses in them. The unit was capable of digging graves and then atomic, biological, and chemical warfare unit also did its share in order to clear up the Vukovar region from all the carcasses. Let me just tell you that out of 15 -- there were actually 15.000 carcasses in the territory of Vukovar and the surrounding area, which is quite a lot. I apologise. If I can say this: The units and the preventive platoon were tasks -- tasked with collecting all carcasses in Jakupovac, Ovcara, and Sutin and hospitalised, if I can say so. Rather, not carcasses but the living animals. They were supposed to capture them, and we managed together to round up 27.000 to 28.000 heads of cattle, and we put them under quarantine, and for several months there was a ban on using those animals until we were sure that they were not infected.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could we see Exhibit 256, please, photograph number 20. ERN number 00531250. Do you recognise the area? Do I need to clarify?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: No, no. This is Ovcara, the region of Ovcara. This is the road leading from the main road to Ovcara, to the administration building, and to the right of the administration building is where we dug large canals, large trenches where we put layers of animal carcasses and then poured lime over it and then finally covered it with soil. We did this both to the left and to the right of the administration building.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could we now have the assistance of the usher, please, so that the witness can mark the areas that he just described as the areas where the carcasses were buried in order to prevent epidemics.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: I saw this area when I toured it, and there was some here too. 1 is the central area, and this is 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't think we will be requiring the assistance any longer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can I tender this marked photograph into evidence, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 761, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We won't be requiring the usher's assistance. Thank you. We won't be requiring it until we have the next photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to turn to the issue of exhumation of corpses, identification of corpses, which was one of the most important tasks of your commission and units subordinated to it. Tell us, please, how did this part of your team function, this part that dealt with locating, exhuming, identifying and marking corpses and then reburying them?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: I have to tell you that that was the most difficult part of our work for a number of reasons, both involving the families of those who died and the victims. And I have to tell you that our most solid work was performed in that area. We worked at Ciglana and we established a large identification station there. There were all kinds of doctors there, surgeons, dentists, pathologists, anybody who we needed in order to identify persons. I have to tell you that we took great care in locating bodies and recording those locations. So we created several documents to that effect. The first document was the document on the finding of the corpse. No military person was allowed to get involved until lawyers and technicians came to the spot and everything was recorded as to what was found on the victim. From that location the corpse was placed into a body bag with certain information and then transported to the identification station. The identification station had the best working conditions. We had heated tents. We had sufficient amount of warm water to bathe the corpses and do everything else, and then there were doctors there who analysed injuries and all other details concerning the death. Then further, we had records on what was found on corpses, and we did this following very strict rules. We had to ensure that everything was done in full compliance. And it lasted for days. People were removing these corpses and taking them to the right place. We also had a location where the corpses were examined, and this is where we wrote post-mortem -- post-mortem records, and then we had all other kinds of records concerning fingerprints, dental records, and so on, in order to ensure that we could better identify these bodies. Victims were, after being processed, put into body bags and then buried at the Bulgarian cemetery, Bugarsko Groblje, with all appropriate dignity and in a dignified ceremony.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You said that before the body was processed for post-mortem examination, it was handed over to investigative organs who performed their work and then -- only then was a post-mortem conducted.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Correct. Crime technicians were there on the spot to give their analysis, their evaluation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Once a body arrived to pathologists for post-mortem examination, were injuries recorded? Did you have any schematic, graphic drawing to record injuries in that drawing?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: This is one of the most sensitive issues. Not only pathologists but also doctors had drawings of human bodies, and they were the ones who entered into the drawing of injuries, whereas all factual details were recorded in the post-mortem record. Yes, this was mandatory. Dental records were recorded there as well. And this is evidenced in the success that we achieved. Namely, we processed 1.300 bodies by December.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes. You mentioned that a large number of persons were identified. Tell me, what did you do about the identified victims? Were families informed or was it not done?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: We had a whole panoply of activities that we conducted. If the person was from the territory of Eastern Slavonia, then, yes, the person's family was informed by Glas Slavonia and then other media. We also had an information bureau at Ciglana, and that functioned very well so that the families would be able to take over bodies as soon as they were available. In the cases where we did not have sufficient information, where the person was not identified, we would bury that body, making sure that whatever records we had were maintained. And if the family was delayed in coming to take over the body, they could pick it up later. It was also possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Does this mean that in relation to each corpse you knew where it was buried, you knew where the information was stored regarding that corpse so that if a family came subsequently you could easily find that corpse and find that information?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. I have to tell you that until late December we held a meeting with military attaches and other international representatives who were relevant where we described to them the work procedure at Ciglana. Major Stankovic held that meeting with them. TV cameras were there. We explained to them the procedure that we used in relation to corpses uncovered in the wider territory of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that these bodies were buried at the Bulgarian cemetery. Can we now see Exhibit 156. This is a map of Vukovar. I think that this is the map of Vukovar in large scale, or in small scale. Yes, we have it on the screen now. Can we zoom into the central area by 25 per cent. No this is too much. This is too much. Can you zoom out. Yes, excellent. Mr. Basic, I guess you are familiar with this map.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Certain areas are marked here.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: On the left side there is the Dubrava forest, and on the right side there is the cemetery right there in the middle.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I want to ask the usher to give you the magic pen again so you can mark the cemetery where you buried corpses that you had exhumed throughout Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You marked it with 1?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mala Dubrava is also interesting because it was extensively mined.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Would you please mark it on the map, this Mala Dubrava area, and put a 2 there.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: These are forest roads, and they were extensively mined.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we tender this map into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you repeat the procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... it will need to be remarked.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We will do it very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Basic, can you mark the Bulgarian cemetery where the bodies exhumed in Vukovar were reburied?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And now 2, next to the Mala Dubrava forest for which you say it was extensively mined.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, Your Honour, I would like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the map marked of Vukovar will become Exhibit 762.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Basic, in the first half of my examination I asked you about Colonel Petkovic and how you reported to him, and he did not want to react. Can you tell us what it was all about? Why did he not want to react? If you can tell us.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Of course I will tell you. I will. When there was this issue with the Chetnik leader Kamena where six people were killed, among them during the night on the eve of new year or thereabouts, I came there urgently. I was there. I could not reach them. There was extensive security, and I asked Petkovic to come there urgently to deal with that. I told you what had happened there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You said that he didn't come?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: No, he didn't come. I went to control this settlement, the Kijena settlement. I could have been killed because I was held at gunpoint and ...

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you one more question, probably my last. Did you ever learn from Colonel Petkovic about the cemetery in Ovcara, that about 200 people had been executed in Ovcara? Did you ever learn that from Colonel Petkovic from Sid?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Let me put it this way: In the territory of Vukovar, I was mostly interested in graves and mass graves. We take a lot of pride that we buried these bodies, that we assist these people regardless of the side that they had been on. We buried everybody with a lot of dignity. That was our utmost priority. However, I'm absolutely certain that if I had known where that grave was I could have exhumed bodies from that grave as well, but I didn't know. I had a few soldiers from the TO who hinted to that, but I did not have the exact information, so I could not know. But I did move around the territory of Jakupovac, but I did not have any information as to where that was, and I could not react.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So you never received any information from Colonel Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: I'm sure that I didn't. Petkovic and I were good pals. That's why our relationship was what it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Basic, for your answers?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, I'm Borovoje Borovic. I represent Miroslav Radic. Your Honour, could we have Exhibit 761 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Do you see this on your screen? A while ago you made some markings on this map. Do you see under 1 where you buried the carcasses and also in the place marked number 2. My question to you is this: Were you the first people to carry out these jobs of clean-up after the fall of Vukovar and Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Was there anybody else that was allowed to do any digging, burying, apart from your commission and your people?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us whether you remember whether in this area that we're looking at the screen on the number 1 where you buried the carcasses, did you find any grave with human bodies or not?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: No, we didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Later on when you finished your job in Vukovar, did you subsequently receive any information as to the fact that across the road from the hangar there was a grave of some sort?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: One more question. When you physically carried out this clean-up and when you dug out the grave for these carcasses, did you find there any empty graves or were there none? Were there no traces of any burials having taken place there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: There was absolutely nothing there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I am asking these questions to explain to the Trial Chamber the reference for my question is on page 5008, line 2, with regard to Witness P022. That is the reference that has made me put this question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Borovic. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no questions for this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Basic, I have very few questions for you, but I think it's right to say that you have indicated what an excellent military record you have. You've excelled in everything that you have done. I think being modest, that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I just ask you about one or two things? You say and have said in your evidence that you have completed the highest possible military schools, including the All People's Defence school. You occupied all positions, platoon commanders up to chief. What exactly does that mean? Can you just give us an idea what your experience was?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you. I am a person with a lot of practice. I was in construction all my life, throughout my career. I acquired knowledge from everybody, from the most common person to the most experienced and knowledgeable person. My experience and the practice that I had helped me to deal with all the problems that I've encountered in my life. I went through all sorts of military schools, the academy, the war school, and this has all helped me to use my knowledge for the well-being of my state which existed at time. At the time, we were all Yugoslavs, let me put it this way. And my view of the territory where I was deployed reflected that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What I'm really trying to clarify is you said that you occupied the position equivalent to that of a general. What exactly do you mean by that, that you had a command structure that operated underneath you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you. In my work, I was held in high regard. I always used my authority as best as I could. Maybe that was my mistake. Maybe I did not call a spade a spade often enough. I had financial recognition that I found satisfactory for the work that I was doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But the question is very simple. Did you have a command structure, a comprehensive command structure underneath you at various times. For example, I think you were a brigade commander between 1976 and 1979. I want to know if you could just tell us what exactly you mean by command structure. What way did it operate?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: I must tell you that a commander is a personality invested with all the responsibility, but a commander cannot work on his own.
