He has his assistants, the chiefs of staff, the assistant for political work, and they all work in a synchronised manner. I always respected these people, and I held their views in high regard. I respected their knowledge, their profession, and everything that could be of assistance to my work. I worked in a synchronised manner with everybody, and that has been a great help to me in my whole life.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that as a commander in, as it was then, the JNA army, that it was important for commanders to coordinate with lesser officers so they understood what was existing within their area of responsibility and their area of command? Would that be a fair way of putting it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And so it would really be a two-way process, I presume. Your subordinates would inform you of what was occurring, and you would, using experience as a commander, observe and make sure that you knew what was going on underneath by your subordinates. Would that again be a fair way of putting it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to ask you about something really to -- to assist me, as I don't really understand it very well. What you say is as follows: "It's pretty clear cut in the army who gives the directives, who hands them out. You have to know what forces are available." I want to deal with if I may with the first part because I don't understand. What do you mean "it's pretty clear cut in the army who gives directives"? What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: I must tell you one thing that you may not be able to understand fully, and that is that the personality of a commander is a personality that is fully capable of command. A commander has to have a lot of characteristics that make him able to command whether he will lead people into war or not, and if people love the commander they will not desert the army, and the commander has to prove himself by his behaviour and by his attitude towards his people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We're just asked, Mr. Moore, to remind the witness to try and speak more slowly because there is difficulty in keeping up with your speed of speaking by the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But it's the phrase that you use, "It's pretty clear cut in the army." What I think you mean is it's pretty clear to the soldiers who's in charge; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you, in the army there's not just one person in charge. We had a system of command in steps, and the commands are handed down, down the ladder, and the one at the bottom of the ladder is the one that is superior to the soldier. And his attitude will also reflect on the commander, but the commander is responsible for the whole system. I occupied a lot of commanding posts, and I had never experienced any confrontation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When you refer to the whole system, I don't come from the Balkan area, I come from the United Kingdom, we did not in our army have anything equivalent to what is called and has been called the security organ. When you refer to the whole system, does that include the security organ?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And when it comes to ensuring that orders are carried out, what methods does a commander of your seniority use to ensure that orders are carried out? What I'm trying to say is you can give an order, but how do you make sure it's acted upon?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: The difference in education between the UK army and our army is very big. I watched movies, I watched relationships, I studied presentations, I followed lectures by officers from those armies. I realised that our system was different. Morale is different. When I was commander, I said to every soldier, "When you see light in my office, that means I'm here. You can bring your parents or whoever to see me." I made sure that the parents of my soldiers dined with them, and I received everybody. There's no recipe, but you have to know that there has to be discipline. That is normal. That is normal across the board, but another thing prevails, and that is love for your commander, love between commanders and soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, can I just set aside love one's commander for a moment and operate on the basis of discipline? Would that be possible? Dealing with discipline, would it be right to say that it is and was an essential element within the JNA army? And we're talking now the 1980s, early 1990s. Would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the last part of your question? Was this the key -- something?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: All I'm suggesting -- maybe I'm going about it in a rather roundabout way. Would you accept that discipline is essential for the existence of any army?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. But how you achieve it is an entirely different ball game.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, let's look at the ball game for a moment. Clearly you have referred to documents and the reporting. So, for example, if a order is issued, it's right to say it can be done in two ways principally, and we're talking 1990, 1991, it can be done orally; is that right? That nod means yes, I presume. And it can be done if written form. That is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Relevant order's always issued in writing. Minor orders are issued orally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, but I mean an unimportant fact like the resubordination of a unit is not important. That could just be done orally, couldn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But you would expect to find that written in the subsequent order to ensure everybody knew where they stood. That's right, isn't it? You've got to know who's underneath you.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: That would be bad practice, if you first issued an oral order and then followed it up by a written order. The essence of most orders and the approach to them is this: Sometimes you don't even have to issue written orders if your officer is responsible. But in any case, if you want to know who is responsible, if you want to assign responsibility to somebody, then yes, you have to follow up with a written order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And why is it important to follow up with a written order? Can you explain to me?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: You see, we are talking about a very significant task if you're referring to the order by the 1st Guards Brigade to the units, which was followed up by the Secretariat for Defence. The second order in this case has to be issued because the latter body was a superior body and the methodology of dealing with the issue contained in the order was different when the subsequent order came from the Federal Secretariat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, that's wonderful, but I'm afraid I've completely lost what exactly your talking about. My question really is very simple. You have told us that if you want to assign responsibility to somebody, then, yes, you have to follow it up with a written order, and I'm asking you why you have to follow it up with a written order. I'm talking about the principle. Why do you use the written order as a follow-up? Why is it necessary?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you one thing. In our command practice, the written order is compulsory up to the level of company commander. From company commander level down, you have oral orders. Orders are transmitted orally. That's the command system we have. Secondly, the person giving an order must also cover everything in an order, because an order can include a great many aspects relevant for whoever is supposed to carry it out. It all depends on the degree of complexity involved in an order. This is a methodology that anybody is free to use to the best of their ability. Sometimes some commanders write their orders down without necessarily envisioning the implementation there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But when we talk about methodology in relation to orders, would it be right to say the more complex the task the more important that there is an order which has specific details outlining the task? I think you've nodded your head, but ...

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Yes, you are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Do you speak English? Okay. You just understand it intuitively.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we just deal then, please, with orders themselves? Why is it important to issue orders on complex tasks?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: It's a little strange the way you're phrasing this question. Every order, especially complex one, must inform the subject about the methodology, about the nature of the order, and a whole series of other matters helping this individual to have the order implemented. An order is never just for an order's sake. That would be the easy way out, to just have it written down. But how exactly do I help those supposed to carry an order out in very practical terms?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let us assume. Let us take you back in time hopefully not very long to where you remember being a brigadier or ostensibly a general. Let us imagine you in that role, that task. You issue a written order. How do you as a brigadier general or a general ensure that that order is carried out? Can you explain that to someone like myself?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Each commander writing an order just to justify his actions without taking into account the implementation stage and without monitoring the implementation stage and without giving practical assistance to whoever is carry it out, well that's something for the commander, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Why is it something for the commander? Please explain.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: I think there should never be an order just for an order's sake. An order must contain practical elements, instructions, what is required in terms of equipment and the exact scope of the task to be carried out by a subordinate officer well-defined. No order is meant forever. The greatest misfortune is that people believe there is such a thing as a recipe for writing orders. There is no such thing as a recipe for orders. It all boils down to the skill and ability of the officer drafting an order. But if you'll excuse me, each subordinate officer is normally familiar and well familiar with their commander, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Ah, you're just talking to a lawyer, I'm afraid. But can we just deal with orders. When you issue an order as a commander, is it important that you familiarise yourself with the environment, the context of the order in relation to what should be achieved? So if something is going to be more difficult, that should be taken into the equation?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: It seems that we are talking at cross-purposes. You cannot have a commander writing for the sake of writing. A commander must be reasonable. He must make sure that assistance is provided through an order to their subordinate officers and to make sure that any mission ordered is successful in terms of implementation. If I don't insist on that, that will soon be the end of me as a commander, because I don't have my own officers making sure that everything is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But what about the subordinate officer whom you give a task to? If the task that is being given to him is either unreasonable, unachievable, then what is that junior subordinate officer supposed to do? Here he is. He's been given an order, but he perhaps doesn't have, as he sees it, the capacity to carry it out. What's the junior officer's responsibility? What should he do in those circumstances? Can you -- can you help me on this?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: We have developed a debate here. We're talking about the framework of command and control. We had a subject talk called command and control for a commander to learn exactly what constitutes good command and good control. If I can't write an order, I'm a poor commander. My superior officer will soon feel the extent of my failure in terms of exercising command and control. If I want my subordinate to get the simplest possible understanding of my order then I should phrase it in such a way that with the least effort expended he understands what it's about. But each subordinate has the right to ask further questions once an order has been seed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What about your situation as a brigadier general or a general, and you receive an order from a superior officer to you indicating an urgent topic or topics that clearly should be implemented at a lower level by units subordinated to you? How do you transmit the urgency or the context or the content to your subordinate officers? Can you explain that to me?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: I must tell you that I faced a situation like that. I was building this road that was to be used by President Tito himself. My deadline is now down to five months. I'm ordering my soldiers, eat -- or, rather, drink your food because you don't have enough time to eat your food. I have to stick to my deadline. Why did I do this? My love for that man, my desire, whatever. But I always found sufficient resources to be able to do that. However, that is no way to go about that sort of task. An officer must be capable. He must know how to give orders, how to receive orders, and how to pass orders down to his own subordinate officers. I must say I'm exceptionally glad to be discussing this matter with you now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I think probably you're the only person, you and I, that are. But can I just go back to the question I asked you, and I asked you is how do you transmit the urgency from your superior officer? Do you -- can you tell us? You get something marked very urgent. It clearly applies to subordinate units. What do you do as a brigadier general or general? I want to know about the methodology that's implied here for command and control of the JNA, and you have that experience. Can you help us?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: I must tell you one thing and one thing alone. We have norms for everything we do, for all the steps we take. We have books containing these norms. It is in the spirit of these norms that we place a soldier, that we place a tank in position, all in the best combat spirit. Improvement can be achieved by using equipment but one of the ways to motivate people is to approach people. This approach, you give them something extra. You give them something that is outside of what would be considered strictly necessary. It's not always like that. You shouldn't think that it's always like that, but there are cases like that and I have had many cases throughout my career.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let me see if I can put it more directly. If you as a brigadier received an order from, let's say, your general informing you that there was a danger of, let us take this context, atrocities, the possibility of atrocities occurring at a lower level. Wouldn't you issue an order immediately transmitting your general's concern? Because if you didn't do so, you wouldn't be carrying out the orders of your general. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: No. The methodology's quite different. You can use knowledge obtained from your closest superiors, from your most intimate superiors, or perhaps you can choose a different methodology. Please, bear one thing in mind. My army commander, I told him, "Sir, General, you can't build a road by using haystacks. You can't do it without money. It's as simple as that."

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What I'm suggesting to you is within the structure of the JNA, if you received an order from your general indicating a topic of concern, you passed it on to your subordinates. Do you agree with that; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: No. You know which method is to be applied to which person. You always use the one you have the most confidence in, and you take one step at a time. There are so many ways to find something out. There are so many ways to obtain certain kinds of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours. I don't have an objection to this question, but I don't think the entire answer has been recorded. He said, "No, not to all, not to all the subordinates." That part was not recorded. And then he continued by saying, "Depending on the method," and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really love your questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You must be one of the very few people who do. Let's -- let's move on. What happens if in actual fact you receive an order from your superior officer, can you disobey it? Can you disobey that order?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: No. There is no such order. You need to approach him to know what is at stake, a case of revolt, a case of insubordination, and then you take further steps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But if you're ordered to -- if as a -- perhaps if I rephrase it. If you receive an order from your superior commander to do something, you're ordered to do it, which would be clear that carrying out that order would involve committing a criminal offence, what do you do then? You can't carry on, can you, because you'll be committing a criminal offence?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: No. Our commanders are reasonable when drafting their orders. We have our commanders. I've had many commanders myself. I spent all my life with commanders, all my career, and I've never seen anything like that happen. There were confrontations. There were considerations to be made, but it wasn't as if I was committing a crime by carrying out an order. It wasn't like I had to be responsible for it. I might as well be carrying out an order by one of my superiors officers but making such omissions in the process that it leads to the same result.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, what I'm going to do is I'm going to read out something to you. You might be aware of it. It's our Exhibit 584. I'm not going to pull it up on e-court. But it's the decree on the declaration of the law on service in the armed forces, February 1985. The sub-heading is, number 2, "Carrying out orders." And it's Article 53. I'll read it out slowly so that you can have it properly translated. It reads as follows: "Members of the armed forces shall be duty-bound to carry out orders issued by their superior officers while their superior officers are in the execution of their office." Now, can we say that we agree with that part, or you agree with that part?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Yes, we do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But it hasn't quite finished. It reads on as follows: "Unless it is clear that carrying out such orders would constitute a criminal offence." Do you agree with that as being a correct statement of carrying out orders? Yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Yes. If you'd read out the entire meaning I would have said yes or no immediately. Yet you read the first half first and only then do you continue with the second half. This is a whole law. You can't have it done by halves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm not trying to do it by halves, I'm merely just breaking it up for understanding. I'm not trying to catch you in any way. I need your help. So you agree that if there was -- the carrying out such orders would constitute a criminal offence, what in your judgement should that junior officer who has received that order do? Can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: You have several methods. He gets back to his superior officer for a report. He seeks an explanation in order to see what he was in for. Further, he can submit a complaint. But one thing that's important in all of this is the relationship between a junior officer and a senior officer with not even the least bit of a spirit of revenge involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm not asking about spirit of revenge. I'm asking you what the duty is. Now, can I just read out the fourth paragraph of Article 53, and I suggest it deals with it. "If he," that's the junior officer, "receives an order and compliance or agreement with that order would constitute a criminal offence, a member of the armed forces shall immediately notify a higher superior officer or an officer senior to the individual who issued the order." Do you agree with that? It seems that it does correspond --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Certainly, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So what it really means is that you are duty-bound to carry out an order unless it's going to involve the likelihood of a criminal act. Do you agree? Yes or no, please?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Certainly. Yes, I do. I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And if -- and if that junior officer believes that that is the case, he basically goes to a superior officer, a superior officer to the one who issued the order. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I asked you about disobeying an officer. If a situation arose -- we deal now with the theory, what I call the JNA command and control climate existing in the 1990, 1991. If an officer receives an order from his superior commander indicating that something is not to be done, not to be done, would it be right to say that unless that officer who receives the superior officer's order, unless he refers either to that officer or a superior officer, he should do nothing except, of course, abide by the order of the superior? It's a convoluted question. I apologise for it, but I think you understand the question. That is right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So if a senior officer indicates no prisoners were to be exchanged without the permission of a superior officer, that should not be done without that senior officer's permission. That is correct, is it not?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. And adopting my learned friend Mr. Borovic's technique, I refer to Exhibit 442, for the Court's assistance. Can I now move off the riveting topic of command and control and deal with one or two other areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would Your Honour forgive me one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, while my learned friend is thinking as to his next move, I am afraid that the tape will run out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Not yet, I don't believe, Mr. Vasic. I would be thinking of a break in about seven minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, I'll try and do a topic within seven minutes if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: We have seen some of the documents and -- dealing with your commission. Shall I just deal with it? Clearly it was a great honour to receive the position you did, running as it is and being responsible for the commission, but what I want to know is if we just deal with Exhibit 758, which is the new exhibit from today, we have got the commission hereby established and made up of. It gives yourself there as chairman, deputy chairman, and there are two members. There is yourself, basically all Colonels, all extremely responsible. Why was there no civilian on that commission?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: A commission is composed of three to five men. Secondly, if the military district commander thinks that his men would be best suited to do the job, he has the right to appoint whoever he wants. I don't have any influence on his opinion. But I believe that the superior command did have a say in the appointment of the commission members.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But I think it's right to say you never suggested the -- because there's only four, we've got one seat vacant, you never recommended a civilian, did you, to come onto your commission, committee? That's right, I think, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: That's true. In any case, there has to be an odd number of people in any commission in order to be able to make decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, there were only four. So if you had another, that would be the odd number, wouldn't it. But in any event, you didn't ask for a civilian. Can I move on to another aspect of the commission itself. That was the -- the terms of reference. I'll use that phrase if I may. What would you say in general terms was the principal term of reference for the -- the role of the commission? What was its principal task?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: I believe that in the documents of the Federal Secretariat you will find the tasks. It's very difficult to prioritise them and say which is the most important. That is why we did not work on just one element. We worked on all the issues parallelly, all the activities relative to identification. De-mining were done at the same time, in the same room.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that often the term of reference don't deal with the reality, but you were there, you knew what the reality was, would it be fair to say that the real job of this commission was to get Vukovar back and running?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You told us about the water supply. You indicated, I think, that the -- you were involved and obliged to bring in water bowsers as I call them, so people could have water to drink. That's right, I think, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Was the water damage -- or was the water supply damaged to such a degree that that was necessary?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: I must tell you that water supply through the town was completely destroyed in many places and that the pipes, the water pipes, had to be replaced because the water system suffered a lot of damage during the war. Everything had to be reconstructed in order to bring the water supply system up to the standard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: If I may pay a small compliment to you. You come across as a senior officer who has integrity. Would you view the targeting of water supplies that were really going to supply civilians, would you take the view that targeting such water supplies would be a breach of all the rules of war?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May I perhaps suggest that that's an appropriate moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will resume at a quarter to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Just a technical issue and a very brief one. We have another witness who is waiting outside, but given the timing, given the fact that my learned friend has asked for another half hour, I would like your permission to send the witness home and start with him on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Your time estimate, Mr. Moore?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: My learned friend asked me how long I would take. I have perhaps three topics. It's difficult to estimate because sometimes the answers and I mean no discourtesy, are not always on point. Perhaps the questions are not always on point. But I would think I would be finishing at half past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The witness will not be reached today, Mr. Vasic. Part of the reason for that, could I suggest, is the questioning in chief this morning dealt with many issues that weren't kernel to the case. So if you could bear that in mind. We're going to simply have to speed up the rate at which we deal with witnesses. Very well. That is the position of the witness Monday. It will be 9.00 morning. 2.15 on Monday, I'm reminded. There were some worried looks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Extremely worried looks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Basic, could I move on to a different topic. What was actually working within the Vukovar infrastructure when you took over 22nd, 23rd? I'm talking about buildings, electricity. Can you just give us an idea?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Yes. Nothing worked save for the logistical support by the assistant commander of the Territorial Defence, Mr. Antic. We had logistical support from them, and there were also some things directly connected with the organisation of life, but very little. We did not even have any support when it came to exhumation and reburials.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I would like, please, just to turn up today's exhibit. I think it is Exhibit 760. It should be the photograph of the bridge or bridges. Here we are. We've got -- have you got it in front of you, Mr. Basic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'm not going to take very long on this topic. We've got the bridges 1, 2, 3 and 4. You were saying that the -- the area, the road up towards the hospital, 4, I think you said was booby-trapped.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But would it be right to say that if you stuck to the road you would have been all right, but don't go off the road? Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: The road itself was not dangerous between the hard shoulders. However, around the department store there was a lot, and a lot around marina. There were a lot of minefields there, and this was the reason for concern. Also, between the department store and the hospital, the park leading up to the hospital was also very dangerous.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May we deal with a topic, I've given a sort of generic title of carcasses, burial of carcasses. You've told us about how many carcasses there were and the need to bury them, and it's right to say that you buried them in the Ovcara area? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I was there when the carcasses were buried. I was interested in the way things were done. I had to gain an impression. This was done by a special unit from Belgrade. The burial was the -- was a minor problem. The biggest problem was to clear up the town and the Ovcara itself where there was cattle moving around in an uncontrolled manner, and that was the biggest problem we faced. You asked me how many head of cattle there were. About 15.000. Pigs and cows. And I can give you a breakdown. Ovcara had 4.500 dead pigs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's very helpful. Perhaps my learned friend may deal with it in re-examination. I won't. Can I move on now to a topic that perhaps concerns this trial a little more than the others, and it is this: It is the bodies of human beings that you were obliged to retrieve and bury. I want to deal with that topic, if I may. So if you can just focus on that. Clearly one of your responsibilities was the collection of those bodies. Yes? Could I just ask you what document you're looking at? Can you just tell me what that is?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: This is the record on the task accomplished about the clearing of Vukovar. This is signed, and one copy was seen to the secretariat. This was signed by the commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And I'm not very good on documents. Do we have a copy of that document, do you know? Apparently Mr. Vasic says that we haven't. Would you have any objection if I have a look at that document? Unfortunately, I don't speak your language, but could I have a look at it for a moment? Do you mind? Could you just pass it over to me? Would you mind? Thank you. That's extremely kind of you. Would Your Honour give me a moment, please. Would you mind if I, with the Court's leave, because it's not an exhibit, but if I gave it to someone trustworthy here to have it photocopied and you could have back the original? You wouldn't mind that, would you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether this document is a classified document. This is my concern. And I sent the document to the Federal Secretariat on the date indicated on the document, and I kept my copy to myself because I was entitled to it. I was the head of the commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I don't criticise you in any way at all. Please understand that. All I'm simply saying is would you mind terribly if I just had this photocopied and you have the original back? I'm asking to be allowed to do that.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you, I don't have the power to allow you to use it without you requesting that officially from the General Staff under a number. I'm sure that they will allow you to have it. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The document was used in court, Mr. Moore. I will have a court officer copy it for the purpose of the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Are there any other documents that you have there? I notice that you have some in front of you that are yellow and look as if they're written records.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What about the -- what about the book that you have? Not that one?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: What you have here?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No, the one that's sitting on the table.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: There's just one page with something written on it. The rest of the book is empty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And the page that is -- has writing on it, what does that page refer to?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: The commission that was in charge of the clear-up, and these are the original words from the minutes. I can quote you what is written in here and you will see that it is identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: All right. I'll not -- I'll not deal with that document for the moment, but let's move on to bodies. Clearly you had, unfortunately, a large number of bodies that were located, and you did your best to identify them and inform the loved ones that their -- someone had been found who had been killed. Was the location of dead bodies a priority for your commission?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: There were three significant tasks pursuant to the document, to collect bodies, to collect cattle in order to prevent infections, and de-mining. Those were the three priorities which were to be followed by the clearing of Vukovar. But the three first tasks could not wait. The others could.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, I just want to deal with the discovery of human bodies. I suggest it was important because clearly the last thing you need from a health position is decaying human bodies or carcasses in a built-up area; and secondly, just for respect for people, to make sure they are given a proper burial. That's right, isn't it, surely? You nod and then we'll put it on the record as yes. Now, you clearly are aware now that there were people who were -- you're clearly aware now that people were murdered and buried at Ovcara. You're aware of that fact? Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No, that's not right, I'd suggest. Are you saying you aren't aware that bodies were found? I'm not talking about you in 1991, I'm talking about now. You're aware that bodies were buried at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: I'm aware now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Now, can we deal, please --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Can I say something, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Of course you may.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: From the press I learnt about Ovcara. There were some Australian journalists who were interested in that. When I came to Ovcara, I didn't know where to go. And then the guards told me to go left. I took that road until I came to the Russian battalion that was providing security for that place. The colonel who was in command there received me, told me that the place was fenced off. He asked me to have a seat, but he did not want to discuss the situation with him, and that was the long and the short of it. Later on, I told you straight and generously that I didn't know a thing. Why wouldn't I have told him if I had known something? If I had known about the place I would have exhumed the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let me ask you to stop, please. You talk very quickly. I'm not suggesting anything about you. I've told you before, I'm not here to trap you. I'm here to obtain information. Do you understand? That is my function. So please listen to the question. You told us that you had heard or you were aware Australian journalists were interested in the killings at Ovcara. I see you nod your head. Can you just say yes so it goes on the record, you see.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: I had already left the army, and as a private citizen I came with them. That was in 1993, sometime in spring. I came there. It took me a while to find the place, and then I was surprised. It was to the very left from the place where we -- where we exhumed bodies. If I had known about that, I could have exhumed the bodies. I could have identified them like all the other bodies that we had found in various burial sites. And this place was some 800 metres to a kilometre from that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'll try and keep my questions short if you try and keep your answers short. I think that's a fair exchange. Would it be right to say, then, that on the record, you were aware, because of Australian journalists in 1993, the suggestion of people being murdered and being buried at Ovcara? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And may we deal then, please, was that something that concerned you, that you had been responsible for the burial of bodies, and here was a suggestion of a large number of people who had been murdered and were buried at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That didn't concern you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Why, because they were Croats?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: No, it's not about that. What I knew about Vukovar was about Vukovar. This was out of the scope of my responsibilities. And if it had been hidden away from me, I could not have known about that. This place Ovcara was something outside of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The area, the actual physical area, was within your scope of responsibility. That is correct, is it not, in 1991?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: If you take into consideration that I was in charge of the downtown area and the general area, then I would say yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So can we just say yes and let's move on a little quicker, please. So Ovcara was within your area of responsibility in 1991, early 1992. Ovcara, in 1993, and we'll just leave it at that moment, there was a suggestion of individuals having been murdered and buried at Ovcara, your former area of responsibility. That is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Because at the time when I arrived there, the place where the burials had taken place that the Russian colonel pointed to me. I saw the area but I couldn't get the impression. The colonel told me that an Australian doctor had arrived and they excavated a skull and that was all. I could not see anything else, and we returned to Belgrade just as we had come there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: We receive from the Defence what is called a proofing note, and that basically means an indication of what your evidence is going to be. Now, it is right, is it not, that you had discussions with lawyers for Mr. Mrksic last evening? That is correct, is it not?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: No. No. I spoke to only one lawyer, Mr. Vasic, and nobody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'll deal with it more specifically. The gentleman sitting there, with the moustache --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: And that was just to prepare me and nothing else. The lawyers did not try to influence me in any way at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I am not for one moment suggesting that Mr. Vasic tried to influence you. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Good.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Good.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And it's right, isn't it, you saw Mr. Vasic last night? That is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And it is correct that you gave an account to him of what had happened. That is also right also isn't?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Not at all?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You didn't discuss -- you didn't discuss this case and what your evidence was going to be?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Of course that we discussed the possible elements. First of all, I was angry that this did not take place at a normal time. I arrived yesterday evening, and they told me, "You would -- you will appear before The Hague Tribunal," and I said, "How? Why?" I had to know what this was all about. You, as a lawyer, must have had a lot of preparation in order to defend your positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm entirely sympathetic to the position that witnesses find themselves in in this Tribunal, so understand that you're speaking to someone who is sympathetic. But the fact of the matter is you did discuss what your evidence might well be. That is correct, under it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So what did you discuss? Just tea and biscuits?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: We had topics to discuss. We had met before. And we never discussed this, in Belgrade or elsewhere. I did not want to waste my time on that. I have my reasoning. I have my own preparations. Why would we have to discuss that? I thought you would talk to me about the impressions of Mr. Sljivancanin and Mrksic. I thought you would ask me to discuss them and not this that you're asking me to discuss.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The questions I ask are a matter for me as long as they're relevant. Do you understand? Now, I'm going to read out what is in this proofing note, which I would suggest indicates what your evidence was going to be. "During the period he," that's you, "worked on the field, the witness said that he found out that some of the volunteer formations had breached the law. On that fact, he had informed Colonel Petkovic in Sid, but the colonel was not apt to take any action." Now, that's -- I won't -- please just don't answer, and I won't ask any questions until the conversation is concluded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: If Your Honour gets the proofing note. I don't know if Your Honours do or not. This is the one that came at 3.50 last night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It may be one you have. It's not one we have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, I've got spare copies. Mr. Vasic, I'm sure, will supply to his colleagues. That's for the Court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I've got it in English. My apologies. I don't know if it's in B/C/S as well. To assist the Court, and I know they like to read it quickly, but if one looks at the very bottom paragraph. May I continue? I'll read it again just to assist all parties and my learned friends. During the period he worked on the field, the witness said that he had found out that "some of the volunteer formations had breached the law. On that fact, he had informed Colonel Petkovic in Sid, but the colonel was not apt to take any action." Now, I would suggest to you that in actual fact there is a very clear indication that when you were in the field in Vukovar you had found out that atrocities had been committed by volunteer formations. Now, what do you say to that? This is a document that's created in relation to the evidence you were to give.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: It's not true at all. Petkovic was never informed, and we talked about that. I'm sorry to say he's to longer alive, but for as long as I knew, he didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I see my learned friend Mr. Vasic wants to interject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, maybe this is something that should be raised if redirect, but I think that the witness is misled, if you followed his evidence, and he talked himself about the information shared with Mr. -- Colonel Petkovic, and I think that follows from his own explanations, the ones that we discussed today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think we better not go into your understanding of facts at the moment. The witness will deal with it, and you can follow it up. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm suggesting that on this proofing note, which is a document created to -- both parties must supply the other side, you see. There is a suggestion, one, that you had found out that volunteers had breached the law, and I would suggest that that means that you found out, either by rumour or by another way, that volunteers had committed atrocities. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: I say this is an untruth and nothing but an untruth. For the first time in my entire career, I can say this: I haven't a clue about this, no clue. It was something entirely different that I discussed with Petkovic, about what happened at the Carrington, and when you brought it up a moment ago, it was the first I ever heard of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I suggest that's not right either, because what you were told in evidence in chief is that you were told by Petkovic about graves. "I had no information." I'm trying to abbreviate from my recollection where it was. "I did have some info in respect of the TO." So did you have a discussion with Petkovic about graves?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, can you explain the following to me, and this is your evidence. What you say is however -- it's 43.20, "However, I'm absolutely certain that if I had known where the grave was, I could have exhumed bodies from that grave as well, but I didn't know." The following phrase: "I had a few soldiers from the TO who hinted to that." Now, what do you mean bit phrase "I had a few soldiers from the TO who hinted to that"? What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: First of all, I wish to say that I did not have any TO in my unit. But in the area where we had our ID station, there were always some TO men. A man named met Metrusic, if I'm not mistaken. He said there's something behind the barracks, there is something we need to look into. But it was so disconnected, so out of context that I didn't pay it any heed at the time. I know that Radio Free Slavonia kept saying that whoever spotted a single dead body should get in touch immediately, and that was a speculation. But I think you misconnected some bits there. The truth of the matter is I called Mr. Petkovic in relation to what had occurred at villa Carrington, not in connection with this. I think you should try to follow more closely. You're misleading me there. Villa Carrington. You know what I'm talking about? Six people -- six men from his group had been killed. That was the problem. You're confusing things there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm not confusing anything, and I'll read it out so there's no misunderstanding what your evidence was. You were actually asked questions by your counsel, and it is as follows: "I would like to ask you one more question, probably my last." That's Mr. Vasic. "Did you ever learn from Colonel Petkovic about the cemetery in Ovcara?" Now, I'm working on the basis that cemeteries doesn't refer to animals. "That about 200 people had been executed in Ovcara. Did you ever learn that from Colonel Petkovic from Sid?" This is your answer: "Let me put it this way: In the territory of Vukovar, I was mostly interested in graves and mass graves. We take a lot of pride that we buried these bodies, that we assist these people regardless of the side that they had been on. We buried everybody with a lot of dignity. That was our utmost priority." Listen now to the following: "However, I'm absolutely certain that if I had known where that grave was, I could have exhumed bodies from that grave as well, but I didn't know. I had a few soldiers from the TO who hinted to that, but I did not have the exact information, so I could not know." That is specifically designed and relates to Ovcara. It's got nothing to do with Velepromet or any other area. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: I think you are totally off the mark. It's got nothing to do with it. It really amazes me that you can act like this. I'm totally clueless about this. You're suggesting that I know about this. How on earth can you possibly know whether I do or not? Please, sir, I'm no clueless brat myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Answer the simple question. Answer the simple question. How is it that that question refers specifically to Ovcara, you refer to TO hints, and you even refer to the grave. Now, explain to me how it is that you give that reply if you didn't know?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: I didn't give anyone that answer. And please don't mislead me on what it was that I was talking about. I'm not sure where you get the idea of putting it to me that I knew. I wish I had known. I wish I'd have been able to do something about it, but I knew nothing at all. Eventually the grave at Ovcara is outside Vukovar. The Bulgarian cemetery marks the end of Vukovar. I'm not saying I wouldn't have done it. I'm not saying I wouldn't have reported it officially. I had no clue. I had no idea, believe me, but you're trying to insinuate that I knew about it, so please don't, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I do suggest you did know, and I'm relying on your evidence, and I would suggest you had a discussion with Petkovic about it and that quite simply the JNA did not want to know about it. That is the reality of this situation.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: That is not the reality of the situation. This is sheer nonsense. I'm not sure where you get this at all. Now you're trying to insinuate something that I wasn't even thinking about, not even in my wildest dreams. How can you possibly be doing like this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm suggesting it because I'm using your words, not anybody else's.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Manipulated ones, twisted ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: They are not manipulated, I would suggest, they are not twisted, and I would equally suggest the reason you're denying it is because you know perfectly well that if you admit that you knew to the grave at that time, that you would be held responsible as well for not passing that information on to superiors. That's why you're denying it. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: I say your illusions are entirely off the mark. It's got nothing to do with the situation that prevailed. Where do you get this information? What can your possible source be? I can tell you that I never had anything to do with this, not even in my wildest imaginings. Why wouldn't I have said so. I didn't even know where it was. I just came there -- I didn't even know where anything else was and you're suggesting I knew. Please, this is simply disrespectful. You are a lawyer. You should know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Moore. Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, let me try to clarify this matter that remains moot. Mr. Vasic, you mentioned a group of people surrounding Kameni; right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You said six people had been killed?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Were these people killed in a clash amid volunteers?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was about the sharing out of their booty but that's something I found out later.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: For you, the murder of six individuals is a crime; right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Yes, definitely a crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Six people were killed, volunteers. For you, that was a crime. You informed Colonel Petkovic; right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Colonel Petkovic did not react, refused to react; right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was on Carrington street. I couldn't go in because I was being held at gunpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: This is the only incident that you reported to Colonel Petkovic as a crime; right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I didn't see him at the time to discuss anything else really.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I would like to move on to something different now. You talked about the way orders were issued. I said orders were issued orally or in writing. My question is if there was an order that was issued orally and it was entered into a notebook belonging to a certain officer, would that have carried the force of a written order?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: No, it wouldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If, for example, an officer orders his subordinate officer to carry out an act which would probably lead to a criminal offence, what about that officer? Would he have the duty to refuse that oral order and ask for the order to be submitted in writing first?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If this officer still believes that this might lead to a crime being committed, he mustn't even carry out at that written order but must, instead, inform his superior officer; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Now, about the water supply system. You said that the destruction of a water supply system constitutes a war crime in your opinion. I would phrase the question in the following way: What about deliberate destruction of a water supply system? Would that constitute a war crime? What if a water supply system is destroyed merely as a consequence of other combat operations and not a deliberate act aiming at leaving people without their water supply?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Yes, you're quite right in suggesting that, and the distinction between these two is enormous.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Were you ever aware of the fact that an infection was rife in Vukovar because of the shortage of water among the population? Those people in the hospital were lying on mattresses stuffed with water after all, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Does that mean you never heard any reference to an infection breaking out in Vukovar during the combat; right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know that during combat in Vukovar they kept on using artesian wells and almost every house had one?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. And we built one such well for the hospital, to be used by the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So your testimony was solely if relation to the town's water supply system, which wasn't operated. Meanwhile the wells and artesian wells continued to be used and operated; right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know where the main water pump of the town's waterworks used to be?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you ever find out if the waterworks facilities had been destroyed by the JNA, or maybe there had been an act of sabotage by the Croatian forces whereby the facilities were destroyed?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: I can't say, but the facilities were entirely disrupted, destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: The facilities were destroyed because they were amid ruins, ruins created by artillery fire; right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: But these ruins could have been caused by booby-traps and by mines, explosives equally; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BASIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasic. Could the Court officer return to the witness the original of the document. The copy held by the Court will be marked for identification, and all counsel have leave to examine that photocopy if they wish.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, it will be marked with the reference number 763, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, you're be pleased to know that is the end of the questions for you. You are now able to return to your home. We would like to thank you for your attendance here and the assistance you have given. And the court officer will show you out. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour. Thank you for the way you have treated me. I wish you every success.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There are some matters that need to be raised now. We had planned by this stage to have dealt with the issue of the length of the Defence cases. The turn of events this week means that I suspect there is not adequate time left at this moment, unless I see on the looks of counsel the thought that it could be dealt with very quickly, and I don't think that is the case. We will simply have to fit it in next week. For that reason and generally, Mr. Vasic, if the Chamber could make clear that it will become imperative for you to be very careful as to the relevance and importance of the matters you deal with with witnesses from now on. We want to get from your witnesses their evidence that is important, but we don't want to have this trial drag on unnecessarily with unimportant and side issues, and we will be much more attentive to interrupting evidence and having counsel move on if counsel are not successful in directing their questions only to important issues. Time is increasingly becoming critical in this case. A problem with that is that the President has called a Plenary meeting for next Wednesday, which means we must try and get into next week the evidence of the witnesses you had planned for the week in four days rather than five. So it will be important for all counsel to be attentive to time. Now, we have just five minutes. Is it that we can successfully deal with the length of the Defence cases in that time? I suspect it's unreasonable and impractical to think of it. So we will defer that issue until next week. Ah, you're showing some hope, are you, Mr. Borovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think we can be pretty accurate in five minutes about our own predictions. That would be useful, useful for me to know what other Defence teams have on their minds. That's efficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will try to meet my learned friend halfway, as well as everybody else in this courtroom, but my Defence case is the first to start, and I hope that I'll be wrapping it up by the end of the first week of October at the latest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And the number of witnesses you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The number of witnesses is in line with our previous predictions, a total of 18, possibly, 19 witnesses. Certainly within that estimate. We've dropped more than half our witnesses who we now believe to be superfluous but we leave the possibility open that we will be further curtailing our list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. As I've already indicated in my motion, we have a total of eight witnesses, two of them 92 bis witnesses. We've taken certain steps already to get their statements signed and accepted by the Court. We have the accused himself, who has decided to appear, and we have an expert. We have a schedule of four hours for each of these witnesses, seven hours in the case of our military witness -- military expert, and 12 hours for the accused himself, which is a total of eight working days. I assume the OTP will not be going too far with their questions, and if we split the time equally, this shouldn't exceed a total of 10 days for all of our witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I make it 16 days on what you've just said. Eight days in chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I said 10 days, I meant the whole thing including the OTP's bit, the total time it would take. If I look at my time only, if I say, for example, 12 hours for Miroslav Radic, what I mean is six hours for the Defence and six hours for the cross. The only thing I can't do is say how long the Prosecution are planning on taking up. And if I may just say another thing. I had been preparing a total of about 20 witnesses, but then I realised what you were saying, that time was of the essence for the accused. I have peared this back down to the bare bones. I have a minimum of witnesses that I require. I have really done my best. I believe that I have achieved most of the things that were essential for our defence with Prosecution witnesses already. I don't think I should go over 10 days including cross-examination as my colleague has just suggested to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you give me a minute and a half, I don't think I'll be able to deal with this, and I certainly wish to have this raised as soon as possible. Your Honour, there is the suggestion that you made at the Pre-Trial Conference. I took it to heart very much so, in fact. I have drafted an overview for that purpose indicating what we believe will be required for examination-in-chief. I would like to provide a table, a copy of this table, for everyone in the courtroom. Ms. Usher, if you could give me hand, and then you could have a look. By Monday -- look at my tentative schedule and then give me five minutes to explain my arguments once you've looked at the table. My Defence case seems to be a very demanding one. It probably requires a greater amount of analysis and in-depth work, especially if I look at the nature of the witnesses I'm calling. I can only draw your attention to one thing, Witness number 2, Witness number 6, Witness number 8, Witness number 9, and Witness number 13 at one point in time gave statements to the OTP, and Mr. Moore can determine confirm this. And these statements ran into 10, 15, sometimes 20 pages, which is a lot longer than the one we took from Vesna Bosanac. And that is something that very much dictates the terms for me in terms of time especially. I think you are fully familiar with some of these names. We're well into this trial, and I believe everybody understands the significance of some of these names and why they would take up the amount of time indicated to testify on behalf of our defence. I dropped witness number 12, and I have a new proposal. I discussed this with Mr. Moore. There are certain witnesses that I wanted to -- to get depositions from, but maybe they could be 98 -- 89(F) witnesses. That would help us avoid their examination-in-chief, and all they would take up is the time that their cross-examination would take. I've tried to be very rational in going through all of these witnesses. If you can give me some more time now or on Monday, depending on the Chamber obviously, perhaps I can go through it and explain in greater detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I am grateful, Mr. Lukic, for the preparation you've done here, but we really are over time now. There is another trial commencing at 2.15 -- not commencing, continuing at 2.15. We simply as matter of courtesy have to leave to give time for the tapes to be replayed and the staff to have a break. So we must adjourn now, but with the information provided now and with opportunity early next week at an appropriate time, we will get to the bottom of this important issue. I'm sure everybody realises it's an issue we can't just put off. It's got to be dealt with if this trial is to be managed sensibly so that we get to its end in a way that deals adequately with the issues but which doesn't just use time wastefully at the cost of the accused, the cost of everybody, and of the cost of the waiting accused. We have trials banked up behind this one waiting. We've got to look at all of those. We will adjourn now. We'll resume on Monday at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 11th day of September, 2006, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.47 p.m.,
